Researchers have been investigating constraint screening, a technique that can expedite the solution process for large-scale unit commitment problems by reducing the number of unnecessary constraints. Current constraint screening methods rely on optimizing load and generation, but this approach tends to be overly cautious and results in a substantial retention of constraints. As a result, the potential screening benefits are not fully realized. To address this limitation, this paper presents an optimized approach to unit commitment constraint screening. By leveraging optimization of both load and generation along with priming, the proposed method significantly improves the ratio of screened out constraints, retaining the feasibility guarantees. Experimental results demonstrate that with this approach, up to $98\%$ of constraints can be screened out without compromising feasibility. Additionally, case studies highlight its potential to accelerate optimization solutions by 1.28 to 2.04 times. Compared to existing methods, the proposed technique retains an additional $4\%$ to $16\%$ of constraints, but provides improved computational efficiency. Consequently, this approach can be applied to various constraint screening algorithms. Moreover, the proposed method enhances the performance of traditional screening algorithms, ultimately enabling the feasibility closure approach to significantly accelerate optimization solutions for large-scale unit commitment problems. This approach is applicable to current state-of-the-art constraint screening algorithms. Finally, the proposed method has been made available on GitHub under the repository \textit{UC1FeasClosures}. By integrating garbage collection with Abstract Interpretation, memory deallocation can be optimized while maintaining an acceptable performance cost, thereby enabling more efficient programs. The study presents a core structure, called Couched, which incorporates both garbage collection and Abstract Interpretation. The Couched framework is based on a model consisting of a set of virtual objects and a pool of physical objects, where virtual objects represent program data structures, and physical objects occupy the actual memory. The Couched structure comprises a pool manager, a set of object fields, and a set of deallocation policies governing when and which physical objects should be reclaimed. The Couched framework is implemented in Chaperone, an open-source library providing efficient refactoring tools for the Scheme programming language. The implementation is based on a refactoring scheme where local data structures, such as lists, are allocated in a stack-like fashion, and global data structures, such as trees, are stored in the heap, allowing for local refactoring of data structures and deallocation of global data when the program terminates. Given the growing shift towards data-driven approaches for dialogue system development, there is now a pressing need to create labelled dialogue datasets that accurately reflect the spoken language habits of users. Previous attempts at collecting such datasets through human dialogue have yielded limited results due to the time-consuming and resource-intensive process, which often results in datasets containing errors. To overcome these challenges, we are proposing a novel crowdsourcing platform called Dialogue Dash that leverages choice-based interactions to collect dialogue data. By presenting participants with dialogue context and multiple choice options, we can ensure the collected data meets pre-defined quality standards, all while reducing the time required per session. Dialogue Dash's effectiveness is demonstrated through a 2-treatment study that compares collected dialogue data for both treatment and control groups in terms of task completion, average session duration, and quality. The results show that Dialogue Dash achieves its objectives, yielding high-quality datasets, and demonstrating the capability to collect more data with fewer resources. Moreover, the data collected using this platform meets quality tests and is shown to have better coherence and consistency compared to systems developed through human dialogue system training. Finally, we showcase a data-driven retrieval dialogue system built using this platform's training data and highlight its performance in achieving a 71.3% completion rate and 0.63 WER on the MultiWOZ dataset. The collected data, Dialogue Dash platform, and accompanying study materials are made publicly available. Through this research, we aim to make spoken dialogue system data collection more efficient, accessible, and user-friendly, ultimately leading to improved system development. By utilizing data from Dialogue Dash to train a retrieval dialogue system, we are able to achieve a 71.3% completion rate and 0.63 WER on the MultiWOZ dataset. To further validate the effectiveness of the platform, we conducted a 2-treatment study comparing the quality and efficiency of dialogue data collected using Dialogue Dash in two different scenarios: using Dialogue Dash with no time limits (SD-NO) and SD with a 30-minute time limit (SD-30). The results show that SD-NO yields higher quality results, but SD-30 still achieves 68.9% completion rate and 0.67 WER on the MultiWOZ dataset. To facilitate future research, we are releasing Dialogue Dash as an open-source platform, along with the collected datasets and the MultiWOZ-SD dataset containing dialogue data collected using this platform on the MultiWOZ dataset. .2-4420, at $z$ = 0.28, contains a unique radio halo surrounding its central cluster core. To explore its development and composition, we examined absorption lines in its spectrum. Our data, obtained from XMM-Newton, Chandra, and Hubble observations, reveal multiple ionized absorption lines, indicating the presence of ionized, warm, and cold gas within the cluster. This system features a radio halo without a central active galactic nucleus, but with signs of a merger between the cluster core and a companion cluster at $\sigma$ = 2.6. The warm phase, with column density log~$\Sigma$ = 17.5-18.2, appears to be linked to the radio halo, while the cold phase, with column density log~$\Sigma$ = 17.2-18.0, aligns with the ionized fraction of the electron density, indicating a shared origin. Both the warm and cold phases exhibit lower ionization than typical, indicating the influence of ionization feedback from the radio source. Our findings suggest that the warm and cold phases have comparable fractions, while the warm phase dominates, accounting for 60% of the total gas. This system displays a higher fraction of warm phase compared to observations of the double beta cluster MS 1455.8+2447. The presence of warm phase gas linked to radio halos may be more widespread than previously thought. To further understand this system, its further observation is recommended. Located at the Laboratori Nazionali di Gran Sasso in Italy, CRESST investigates dark matter through the use of highly pure crystals that act as highly sensitive detectors to record the occasional nuclear recoil triggered by a dark matter particle interaction with a detector nucleus. With a focus on isotopes that have a non-zero spin quantum number, CRESST employs the time resolution capabilities of its crystal detectors to differentiate between interactions resulting from alpha particles and neutron scattering. Inside a vacuum tank, the experiment's wafer-sized crystals are surrounded by a thin layer of enriched $^{160}$TiO$_2) with a 40 mm thickness and 600 g mass, and in conjunction with other detectors, temperature data from multiple types of crystals can be used to differentiate between interactions. With an analysis period spanning from 2017 to 2018, CRESST achieved a time-dependent sensitivity to spin-independent dark matter cross-sections that extends to higher masses than before, and with further optimization and analysis, the experiment aims to reach a time-dependent sensitivity to dark matter cross-sections of less than $10^{-17}$ pb at a mass of $10^4$ GeV in the future. In addition to its dark matter investigation, CRESST has also made significant contributions to neutrino research by analyzing oscillations and their impact on detector mass. in waveguide QED systems, focusing on systems that can be spatially localized. We begin by introducing the principles and advantages of employing diagrammatic methods in these systems, which involve the use of bosonic and fermionic diagrams to represent physical processes. These principles are illustrated through the analysis of two key systems: an isolated atom and a molecule in contact with a waveguide edge, characterized by nonlocalizable bosonic and fermionic processes. We then introduce the concept of normal products, which enables the derivation of an effective Hamiltonian for these systems and their response to strong light-matter interactions. Our results demonstrate that normal products can be defined up to a constant that depends on the system's initial state, thus retaining key physical insights. We conclude by presenting an alternative approach, which involves the use of time-averaged normal products and an effective Hamiltonian for time-periodic systems. Our findings are verified by comparing the derived effective Hamiltonians with exact numerical calculations for both the two-level atom and the molecule. We also discuss the potential applications of diagrammatic methods in waveguide QED systems, encompassing the analysis of non-Markovian dynamics, the derivation of dressed dispersions, and the description of nonlocal responses using normal products. Ultimately, these methods can be extended to more complex, spatially localized systems, which are essential for the development of compact and efficient quantum technologies. In particular, we present a detailed analysis of a linear chain of atoms coupled to a waveguide, which is crucial for the realization of quantum circuits and is characterized by nonlocal bosonic and fermionic processes. In the context of unsupervised domain adaptation, balancing classification accuracy and inter-domain similarity is crucial. However, these objectives often conflict, and optimizing one may compromise the other. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a new bi-level optimization framework that produces a shared latent space among multiple target domains. By initially aligning individual domain adaptation models through a patient teacher approach and then consolidating their features, we can achieve a shared latent space that strikes a balance between classification accuracy and inter-domain similarity. We also establish a comprehensive evaluation framework for multi-domain NLP models by categorizing various multi-domain models into three types: multi-domain model pre-training, multi-sample data augmentation, and multi-task learning. We've found that this support comes with a hidden cost: when these states are measured, the expected outcome isn't solely dependent on the applied gauge potential. Instead, the quantum fluctuations of the potential itself play a significant role. This effect has a substantial impact on the accuracy with which certain quantum simulations can replicate a given quantum system. Our analysis specifically examines a universal emulating process for an arbitrary 1D quantum system. By investigating the emulating gauge potentials generated by different methods, our research reveals that the performance of these potentials is ultimately limited by their variance. We've demonstrated that the maximum success rate of teleporting an arbitrary 1D quantum system is directly related to the variance of the gauge potential used in the process. We've also shown that this rate has a theoretical maximum limit, representing the best possible outcome in terms of both success rate and transmitted fidelity. This optimal success rate corresponds to the average fidelity of the gauge potential used. We've further explored the implications of these results in the context of a specific quantum teleportation scenario involving a hard-core boson lattice. Utilizing a two-dimensional path-integral method, our research reveals that achieving high transmission fidelity is inherently difficult. However, our study also shows that it's possible to achieve significant transmission by focusing on lower-dimensional processes. This, in turn, allows for the successful transmission of an arbitrary quantum system, despite the variance of the gauge potential used. We've demonstrated the practicality of these concepts through a real-world example involving the quantum simulation of a 1D Fermi-Hubbard model using a digital quantum simulator. We conducted a study using the HRSC simulation method, specifically exploring the dynamics of accretion and ejecta during the merger of a black hole and a neutron star. Our simulations reveal that the accretion of the neutron star onto the black hole occurs in two stages: initially, the neutron star is ejected with low angular momentum, but it eventually spirals into the black hole due to gravitational torque. As a result, a disk forms near the black hole with a mass equivalent to about one-thirty-second of the neutron star's mass. This disk leads to the launch of winds that carry a magnetic rotation measure of the order of $10^2-10^3 \ \rm cm^{-1}$, which could explain the appearance of transient radio pulses similar to SGRB 160410B. Our models also demonstrate that the ejecta from the dynamical ejecta and the disk winds have sufficient kinetic energy and magnetic field strength to form a relativistic jet, which could travel a distance of several hundred megaparsecs. However, this jet would face significant magnetic braking, reducing its opening angle and magnetic field strength by several orders of magnitude. The relativistic jet would then interact with the circumstellar medium, producing radio flares similar to GRB 130909A. Our models suggest that the launch of the jet from the accretion and ejecta is a plausible explanation for the late-time radio emission in some SGRBs and GRBs. However, this jet would need to remain confined to a narrow opening angle of about one degree in order for its travel distance to be within the range of typical short gamma-ray burst sources. This implies that the magnetic field within the jet would need to be significantly weaker than what is observed in the initial winds. Furthermore, the relativistic jet would need to be stable over a long period of time, and the accompanying wind would need to be re-accelerated to achieve its destination. The launch of the jet from the accretion and ejecta is therefore a promising explanation for late-time radio emission in short gamma-ray bursts, but further studies are required to confirm the necessary conditions. To fill this void, we have developed FastNLO, an open-source software library for rapid modeling of chirped pulse amplification and nonlinear optical systems, and its associated system. By applying a novel single-qubit rotation to the input states, we demonstrate that any unitary transformation within the qubit space can be optimally measured using either Pauli or Hadamard operators, thereby enabling a more efficient measurement process. To overcome this challenge, companies are turning to technology to their aid. By leveraging cutting-edge communication tools like video conferencing software, virtual collaboration platforms, and social networking apps, they can create a sense of unity and inclusiveness that bridges the gap between remote workers and fosters a strong company culture.

In this article, we will delve into the world of remote working, exploring its benefits, drawbacks, and the innovative technologies being used to support it. We will also examine the future of remote working, including the promising prospects that lie ahead, such as the rising trend of No-Face Job (NFJ) working, in which individuals can choose from a range of flexible, non-traditional work options.

In the final section of this article, we will explore some potential innovations that could further transform the future of remote working, from Augmented Reality to Artificial Intelligence. By combining the power of human creativity with the capabilities of AI, we can unlock new possibilities for remote collaboration, creativity, and innovation. 

Ultimately, as we embark on this journey into the future of remote working, we will reflect on the significant impact it can have on our personal and professional lives, our relationships with technology, and our aspirations for a better future. increasingly larger numbers of cryogenic qubits in quantum computing applications is driving research for an optimal solution.  We present an innovative compact cooling concept that efficiently cools multiple qubits simultaneously, effectively minimizing the substantial heat leakages associated with cryogenic qubits due to their low operating base temperature and high thermal conductivity.  Our design consists of a single silicon carbide (SiC) thermal sink that supports a network of thin, thermally conductive 'whiskers' which enhance heat transfer to a nearby 250 mK cold plate, and has been shown to cool loads of approximately 1 millikelvin above the cold plate's temperature in both experimental and simulated tests.  Our results indicate that this cooling architecture's thermal limited performance is primarily defined by the thermal properties of the cold plate, and outperforms previously predicted values based on copper thermal sinks by an order of magnitude.  Furthermore, this cooling architecture's thermal limited performance is largely independent of the cooled system's complexity, and offers the potential for significant improvements over current quantum computing cryogenic qubit cooling systems.  We propose that this cooling concept could be developed into a standardized, factory-producible cooling solution that could be used across various cryogenic quantum computing applications, and serves as an important step towards the development of practical large-scale quantum computers.  Our design has also been submitted to the US Patent Office under the reference PCT/US2021/051637.  We have also made available the detailed design specifications, 3D models, and simulation code for this cooling concept in our GitHub repository at https://github.com/joshuaflorescooling/.  Finally, this cooling concept has the potential for further improvement through the use of advanced materials such as future generations of super-black silicon carbide, and future iterations of this concept could also incorporate additional features such as further thermal improvements, improved mechanical design, and the integration of proximity-proximity sensors for enhanced error correction in quantum computing applications.  We have also made available a video explaining this innovative cooling concept at https://youtu.be/8Q8Q6Q6Q6Q6. This concept is known as the $R$-sequential problem or the Sequence Color Problem. For a given graph $G$ and its coloring properties, the Sequence Color Number $\sigma_G(t)$ represents the largest order $k$ for which a $R$-sequential $t$-coloring of $G$ exists. This work focuses on determining upper bounds for $\sigma_G(t)$. For any graph $G$ and integer $t$, it has been proven that $\sigma_G(t) = O(t^{(d+1)/d})$. To contribute to the development of such technology, this study demonstrates an innovative method for producing microwave frequency lasers, or parametric amplifiers, through the application of Josephson junctions and magnetic flux triggers. The design incorporates a single control loop and magnetic flux trigger to activate an inductive loop, connected in series to a resistive loop and an RC circuit. When a magnetic flux threshold is reached, the inductive loop produces a current through the RC circuit, resulting in non-linear amplification of microwave frequency inputs via the parametric amplification phenomenon. The single-control-loop design enhances stability while the use of resistors and inductors allows for easier tuning of amplifier frequencies. The system's effectiveness as a parametric amplifier was demonstrated by its ability to amplify microwave frequency noise, achieving an impressive gain of 4.1 times the input signal. The same design can also function as a microwave frequency laser by reaching steady-state in the RC circuit, resulting in sustained amplification of noise, typically, several orders of magnitude stronger than the input signal. The ability to reach steady-state depends on the balance between the decay rates of the RC circuit components and the gain provided by the parametric amplification. By fine-tuning the ratio of inductors and resistors, the frequency at which the parametric amplification reaches its maximum rate of change can be adjusted, thus allowing for further amplification of the laser output when triggered by the correct magnetic flux. The single-control-loop design enables easy access to the parametric amplification rate of change, making it possible to implement a feedback loop and achieve precise control over the microwave frequency lasers. This model, inspired by the thermodynamic concept of dissipative systems, ensures its constitutive equations are in harmony with standard principles of thermodynamics. It is acknowledged that a completely accurate mathematical representation of a material's frictional behavior may be unattainable. Instead, our model treats the standard friction laws as approximations, allowing for continuous improvement as more accurate descriptions are discovered. We provide a general framework for various friction laws and multiple material behaviors, including rate-independent and dissipative materials, along with those exhibiting memory and those that do not. We also establish the necessary conditions for the model's constitutive equations to be physically valid and provide a set of criteria to determine if a given friction law meets these requirements. We present two numerical examples to demonstrate how this model can be numerically implemented and provide a basis for evaluating the accuracy of approximated friction laws. These examples involve simulating static friction between two blocks and a block under varying vertical loads, using two different friction laws: the standard Coulomb friction law and a novel logarithmic friction law. We verify that both simulations satisfy the principle of energy conservation and observe the logarithic friction law's influence on the stress and deformation tensors of the blocks. We show that the logarithmic friction law produces stress and deformation patterns that are qualitatively and, in some cases, nearly identically similar to those obtained using the standard Coulomb friction law. This suggests that the standard Coulomb friction law may be an effective approximation of a more complex, but unattainable, friction law. We conclude that the proposed model offers a flexible and efficient framework for the numerical analysis of frictional materials and provide a starting point for the creation of more advanced material models that take into account the history of strain path progression and frictional dissipation. We highlight the model's potential to be used in various engineering applications, such as the numerical simulation of geotechnical structures, and suggest that a more in-depth numerical analysis could reveal the logarithic friction law's influence on the material's behavior. Additionally, we note that a more sophisticated friction law could potentially be discovered, and we propose that a more accurate description of friction may exist and can be identified through the use of machine learning techniques. A recent study from TU Berlin's research team analyzed the performance of different Natural Language Processing models on Subtask 2 of Interspeech 2021, which focused on recognizing hate speech tweets. Our team aimed to compare the effectiveness of distinct neural network architectures, including transformer-based models, and varied the training data by 3, 10, and 20% while utilizing data augmentation and weighted binary cross-entropy. Notably, our results show that higher training data does not necessarily lead to improved accuracy; rather, a 3% training data yield surpassed the performance of 10% and 20% training data in this specific context. Additionally, a well-known German-NLP model demonstrated inferior accuracy compared to a basic transformer model. Ultimately, the best-performing model achieved a precision, recall, and F1 score of 0.88, 0.84, and 0.86, respectively, but when expanded to 100 models, a higher precision and recall were reported at 0.855 and 0.837, respectively. Although a natural extension of basic networks, pre-trained MIMO models have not consistently led to better performance. This paper investigates ensemble dynamics to explain this inconsistency. By analyzing network behavior, we discover that MIMO architecture is ill-suited for handling correlations between inputs and outputs, which are common in real-world datasets. We employ a technique to segment uncorrelated sub-inputs from the training data and reorganize the input to optimize network features. Our method, named Kardano, significantly improves ensemble model robustness on multiple benchmark datasets and achieves consistent top results on image and language processing tasks, outperforming traditional ensemble models in most cases while exceeding the performance of MIMO models when individual models are highly accurate. A combination of cross-sectional surveys and longitudinal studies in low- and middle-income countries, namely the Global Burden of Disease Study and the Prospective Urban and Rural Epidemiology (PURE) study, were utilized to investigate the natural history of four major non-communicable diseases - heart disease, stroke, cancer, and diabetes.

Data analysis revealed that a substantial portion of individuals in low- and middle-income countries experience the onset of these diseases at an early age, with notable trends observed. For instance, the likelihood of heart disease and stroke being diagnosed before the age of 60 is particularly high in low- and middle-income countries, whereas early-stage cancer detection is more prevalent in low- and middle- income countries, with around 45% of cases compared to 35% in high-income nations.

However, individuals in low- and middle-income countries face a higher mortality rate from these diseases at a younger age. A key finding was that a substantial death toll from these diseases occurs before the age of 60, with approximately 41% of heart disease, 42% of stroke, and 39% of cancer-related deaths occurring at this age in low- and middle-income countries, resulting in a significantly shorter life expectancy as compared to high-income nations.

These findings highlight the pressing need for early intervention and prevention strategies to mitigate the onset of these diseases at a younger age in low- and middle-income countries. Moreover, there is a necessity for developing effective treatment and care pathways to enhance survival rates and life expectancy in these countries. The study's results can serve as a foundation for policy-making and clinical decision-making to reduce the burden of non-communicable diseases in low- and middle-income countries. In comparison to other top challenge participants, K-Means ETM achieved comparable results to model 4-4-2-1 with an increase of 1.51% in accuracy and a decrease of 0.51% in precision, along with other minor differences. 
The proposed K-Means ETM approach offers a straightforward and efficient solution for retinal diabetic detection.

Health Records (EHRs) has captured the interest of the research community, although the complexity of annotating these records with medical diagnoses is still a major challenge. This difficulty stems from the necessity for medical experts to review entire patient histories, necessitating a task necessitating extensive reading. This study presents a novel approach to mitigate the requirements of annotation. Instead of labeling individual patients with medical conditions, we propose a simplified system where annotators provide a concise summary of the most significant medical issues, reducing the number of possible annotations from thousands to approximately two hundred. This approach is based on the pre-existing Medical Condition Ontology. Our experiments demonstrate that this method of reduced annotation complexity can be effective, using a human-only panel, and is comparable to the traditional method with regard to machine learning performance. This approach is expected to significantly decrease the time and effort required for annotation, thus facilitating the utilization of EHRs in clinical decision support systems. These models are typically multi-agent in nature, with agents exhibiting a mix of innate and learned behaviors. While multi-agent modeling via ordinary differential equations is feasible, it can be challenging due to the sheer number of parameters required. To overcome this limitation, this study proposes a new framework for modeling human behavior using neural ordinary differential equations, a type of multi-layer perceptron. By applying this approach to two well-established models, this work demonstrates its potential for improving model accuracy and facilitating learning from real-world data. Furthermore, NOE's differentiable nature enables the analysis of various model parameters, such as initial conditions, network architecture, and data quality. This study's results indicate that the key factor influencing model performance is data quality. Consequently, the research presents a method for assessing raw observational data for its suitability in training neural models. By combining a data-driven uncertainty analysis with a multi-agent ODE model, this work shows that poor-quality data can significantly impede the learning process. To address this issue, the research proposes a data pre-processing technique that enhances data quality through a statistical analysis of the data's information content. By applying this approach to two data sets, this work demonstrates that the resulting pre-processed data can effectively support neural network learning. Moreover, the research presents a new approach for modeling complex multi-agent networks with spatial relationships. By combining convolutional neural networks with graph theory, this work introduces graph-based initialization and pooling techniques for spatial data handling. By applying this approach to a multi-agent model, this work demonstrates its potential for improving model accuracy and facilitating spatial data analysis. Overall, the research presents a set of novel methodologies for multi-agent modeling that are grounded in neural ordinary differential equations and the application of advanced machine learning techniques. These novel approaches have the potential to significantly enhance our understanding of complex social networks and their dynamics. Suppose we have a set of $m$ statistical hypotheses denoted as $\mathcal{H}_1, \dots, \mathcal{H}_m$, as well as corresponding test statistics $T_1, \dots, T_m$, which are used to assess the validity of these hypotheses. Typically, each statistical hypothesis is associated with a null limit distribution, denoted as $F_1, \dots, F_m$. However, storing the null limit distributions for each test can be computationally expensive and require significant storage space. Our paper proposes an efficient statistical testing framework that can determine whether statistical hypotheses are valid without needing to store the null limit distributions. 

We establish a two-stage testing framework, starting by performing initial tests on all hypotheses. Then, for each hypothesis, we estimate the null limit distribution using the retained test statistics and generate a null distribution specifically for that hypothesis. This approach ensures that hypothesis-specific calculations are performed, which is crucial in non-parametric settings. 

Our testing framework is versatile and can be applied to both parametric and non-parametric hypotheses. Our results demonstrate that the family-wise error rate and the false discovery rate are strongly controlled under certain conditions. We apply our framework to multi-variable, high-dimensional linear regression models, achieving strong control of the false discovery rate. A multi-stage procedure is also introduced for implementing our FDR control methods. Our approach is evaluated through simulations and real-world data. 

The framework appears at arXiv:2012.07113.

nostic Reinforcement Learning involves achieving robustness against manipulative opponents who can alter environmental dynamics and reward structures at will.  In our research, we introduce a strong model for the learner to contend with such adversaries.  Under the assumption that the learner has a comprehensive understanding of the environment's dynamics, we establish a robust optimality criterion that ensures the best outcome in the most unfavorable scenario.  However, this condition becomes computationally impractical when the number of possible environmental variants expands exponentially.  In response, we present a robust optimality criterion under approximate uncertainty about the environment's dynamics, limited to a finite set of possibilities.  We break down the trade-off between robustness and performance using this condition and identify a specific performance threshold below which robustness can be improved regardless of performance gains.  We demonstrate the value of our model through experiments in Markov Decision Processes.  In scenarios where the adversary's actions are limited, we achieve robustness without sacrificing performance.  In contrast, we show that our model allows for significant performance losses when approximating uncertainty does not accurately reflect the actual uncertainty.  We hope that our research will serve as a foundation for future studies on robust robust Markov decision problems.  In particular, we identify open challenges related to non-stationary environments and non-Bayesian uncertainty models.  In addition, we outline potential approaches for addressing robust robust Markov decision problems, including non-cooperative games and agnostic Reinforcement Learning.  In contrast to these approaches, we show that our model offers a more general and comprehensive robustness condition, surpassing previous models that assume explicit knowledge of the adversary's reward structures.  In particular, we improve upon the robust optimality criterion introduced by Lin et al. in 2021, achieving robustness without sacrificing performance when approximating uncertainty matches the actual uncertainty.  In addition, we show that our model is compatible with various existing algorithms for robust Reinforcement Learning. This restriction significantly impacts their potential to handle longer texts, which often necessitates more complex transformations. To address this challenge, we propose a new set of scalable text transformations that can effectively process longer input sequences. These transformations are based on the concept of tesselations - the process of dividing a sequence into multiple copies of itself to facilitate repeated applications. Two types of tesselating transformations are introduced: block Kornai-boxes and 1-diffusion. We showcase the utility of these transformations through the creation of two innovative text mutators that successfully passed the blind NLP mutator challenge, achieving state-of-the-art results on multiple metrics and extending the input data coverage to previously unexplored regions. Furthermore, we provide an open-source implementation of the proposed tesselating transformations, enabling their direct integration into existing word-level NLP mutators. This implementation is available at https://github.com/kuangkul/telex. The experiments demonstrate that the developed tesselating mutators can produce a significantly larger variety of text than traditional mutators, with up to an 8-fold increase in the number of unique words generated from a given input. These findings suggest that tesselating mutators can serve as a more effective exploration method for word space search, potentially uncovering novel and interesting word forms. To facilitate further research, we provide an interactive visualization tool that allows users to explore the word space search results, including a new region of the 1D word space containing over 100 words that were not known to us at the time of the experiment. Importantly, our results demonstrate that these novel words are located closer to the original query word, rather than spreading out across the word space, indicating that tesselating mutators can indeed be an efficient discovery tool. Lastly, we propose a new evaluation metric to assess the quality of text mutators by measuring how well they preserve semantic relationships within the mutated text. The results show that tesselating mutators can achieve state-of-the-art results on this metric, further highlighting their potential to preserve crucial semantic information during text transformations. The experiments also reveal that combining tesselating mutators with non-tesselating mutators can further improve the ability to preserve semantic relationships, underscoring the potential of our approach to revolutionize data augmentation methods in NLP.
